method: Offsets are converted to minutes and the wall-clock change is the destination offset minus the origin offset; a New York (-5) to Tokyo (+9) trip is +14h, or 840 minutes. Because the body clock can adapt in either direction, the planner reduces that change to the shorter way around the clock: any result above 720 minutes is replaced by itself minus 1440, so +840 minutes becomes -600, a ten-hour delay. The sign names the direction of the bedtime move: positive means advance (sleep earlier), negative means delay (sleep later), and exactly 720 minutes is treated as an advance. A forced advance or delay keeps that direction and takes the long way round instead, so the same trip forced to advance is a 14-hour shift. The shift needed is divided by the days available to give the daily step, which is capped at the user's maximum per-day value; if the cap binds, the full shift simply takes ceil(magnitude / daily step) days and the result says so. The arrival bedtime is the habitual bedtime plus the signed body-clock shift, shown modulo 24 hours in destination local time, and the wake time keeps the same sleep-window length. The schedule starts at day 0 (arrival day) with the whole body-clock offset applied and moves the bedtime one daily step toward the habitual local bedtime on each later night; at most the first 15 nights are listed. Inputs are limited to offsets from -12 to 14 hours and daily steps from 0.25 to 4 hours in quarter-hour increments, 1 to 30 days and 24-hour HH:MM sleep times, and every message names the field and its range. This is time arithmetic for planning, not medical advice, and individual sleep patterns vary. Everything runs in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: UTC offsets range from UTC-12:00 to UTC+14:00, and some zones use 30- or 45-minute offsets such as Nepal at UTC+05:45 and Eucla at UTC+08:45.

A time-zone change shifts the sleep schedule by the offset difference; the two ways around the clock are the difference itself and 24 hours minus that difference, and the smaller one is the shorter adjustment.
Jet lag plans spread the adjustment over several days with a limited daily step rather than jumping the whole offset on the first night.
